parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: amplitude as maximum displacement from equilibrium
period as time for one complete oscillation
hints: Hint 1: Look at the $x$-$t$ graph and think what the tallest peak tells you about how far the object goes from $x=0$, and what the time between two identical neighbouring peaks tells you about how long one full swing takes.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading Amplitude From the Peak**
You are looking at a displacement-time graph for SHM. Amplitude $x_0$ is simply the maximum distance from the equilibrium position $x=0$. Here the curve just touches $1.8\text{ cm}$ at the top and $-1.8\text{ cm}$ at the bottom, so $x_0 = 1.8\text{ cm}$.

Step 2: **Reading Period From the Repeat Time**
Period $T$ is the time for one complete oscillation, for example from one maximum to the next maximum. The first maximum is at $t=0$ and the next maximum is at $t=0.30\text{ s}$, so $$T = 0.30\text{ s}$$

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: unit conversion g to kg and cm to m
hints: Hint 1: First read the displacement $x$ at $t = 0.19\text{ s}$ directly off Fig. 4.1, and remember that in SHM kinetic energy is largest at $x=0$ and zero at $x = \pm x_0$.
Hint 2: Recall that $\omega = 2\pi / T$ and that kinetic energy can be found from $E_K = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2(x_0^2 - x^2)$. Check all your units are in kg and m before you calculate.

Hint 3: Use $m = 0.080\text{ kg}$, $x_0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ and your value of $|x|$ at $0.19\text{ s}$ of about $1.2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ to evaluate the expression and give $E_K$ in J.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Where the Object Is at 0.19 s**
Slide your eye up from $t = 0.19\text{ s}$ on the time axis to the curve. The object is on its way back up from the trough, at about $x = -1.2\text{ cm}$. For energy only the magnitude matters, so use $$|x| = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$ with amplitude $$x_0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Get Angular Frequency**
SHM oscillates with angular frequency $\omega$ linked to period $T$ by $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ With $T = 0.30\text{ s}$: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{0.30} \approx 20.9\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ This tells you how fast the phase changes.

Step 3: **Use the SHM Energy Formula**
Total energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$ and potential energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$, so what is left is kinetic: $$E_K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(x_0^2 - x^2)$$ Convert mass: $m = 80\text{ g} = 0.080\text{ kg}$. Then $$E_K = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.080 \times \left(\frac{2\pi}{0.30}\right)^2 \times [(1.8 \times 10^{-2})^2 - (1.2 \times 10^{-2})^2]$$

Step 4: **Calculate the Value**
Evaluating gives $$E_K \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$$ This makes sense: the object is quite close to the extreme position where speed is small, so the kinetic energy is only a fraction of the maximum $\tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$.
